thought.text: PHP-FPM is running. Now let me deploy the app to the nginx document root, following the guide (top-level folders + HTML pages + examples).

reasoning_content:
PHP-FPM is running with the socket at /run/php/php8.1-fpm.sock. Next, deploy the application to the document root.

Deployment plan following the guide:
- To /var/www/html, copy: config, externalPackages, i18n, src, php, data (top-level), plus the top-level HTML pages (index.html, csvParse.html, elasticsearchIndexAdministration.html, plausibilityCheck.html), logo.png.
- Also, deploy a few pages from examples? The guide says that pages inside examples need to be copied to the docroot, and that they'll work there. But note: some example pages have their own local config/, src/, externalPackages/ directories (komono, kontoauszuege, spotify, kosis, treeCadastre have their own config/ and src/). If you copy those pages to the root, they'll reference the root-level config/src/externalPackages (e.g., komono's index.html uses relative paths externalPackages/..., src/...). So that's fine — they'll use the root copies.

Actually, wait, komono/index.html references `config/baseConfig.json` — relative to the docroot, so the root config/baseConfig.json. OK.

Simplest approach: copy everything (the entire project directory) to /var/www/html. This satisfies "add the following folders to the document root folder" and also covers the examples subdirectory (the guide says pages inside examples subfolders will work — but since the pages use relative references, they'll find their own sibling directories… no, wait! If komono/index.html is at /var/www/html/examples/komono/index.html, it'll look for /var/www/html/examples/komono/config/ — that exists locally. If it's copied to /var/www/html/komonoIndex.html, it'll look for /var/www/html/config/ — that also exists. Either way, it works.

The guide says to copy the HTML pages you want to provide to the same folder. To keep it clean and stay true to the guide, let's do the following:
- cp -r config externalPackages i18n src php → /var/www/html/
- mkdir -p /var/www/html/data (top-level data folder; the guide says "additionally, the top level needs a folder _data_" — the repo doesn't have a top-level data/; it's created for a specific instance)
- Top-level HTML pages + logo.png → /var/www/html/
- Copy some example pages to the docroot: the kosis pages (kosisDemo.html, kosisMap.html, kosisPredefinedQueries.html, kosisCsvParse.html, landingPage.html, xmlParse.html) — kosis is the flagship example. But wait: the kosis pages reference local config and data, right? Earlier when I grepped kosis's HTML, I didn't find any fetch to data/. The kosis page references config/baseConfig.json (relative) — if I copy it to the docroot, it'll use the root config. Good.

Also, I could copy the komono page (index.html → komonoIndex.html?). Hmm, if I copy the file index.html from komono to the root, it'll collide with the root index.html! The root index.html is "Data Explorer" (the generic version). komono's is the "Kaiserslautern Komono" instance. To avoid overwriting, I need to rename. Let me name them komono.html etc. The guide says the pages are "functional there" as long as the file references are relative — renaming is fine.

Which pages to copy to the root? What I'll pick:
- Top level: index.html, csvParse.html, elasticsearchIndexAdministration.html, plausibilityCheck.html
- kosis: kosisDemo.html, kosisMap.html, kosisPredefinedQueries.html, kosisCsvParse.html, kosisDumpParse.html, xmlParse.html, landingPage.html (keep the name landingPage.html — there's no collision at the root; no, wait, is there a landingPage.html at the root? No, the root has index.html, csvParse.html, elasticsearchIndexAdministration.html, plausibilityCheck.html. OK, no collision.)
- komono: index.html → komono.html
- spotify: indexSpotify.html
- kontoauszuege: indexKontoauszuege.html, search.html
- fcd: csvParseFcd.html
- treeCadastre: all 4 pages

Hmm, this is a lot. But it's simple file copying, so it's fine. In fact, the guide says "copy the HTML pages you want to provide to your Explorer instance." For a complete installation, providing the entire set is the most faithful interpretation, and it also serves as a functional demo.

But wait — the pages in the examples subdirectories also work if they stay in their own directories (that's the "proper use case"). The most faithful deployment might be to copy the entire repository to the docroot. That way, everything works in both ways. The repo is small (let me check the size). externalPackages and the per-example copies of it might bloat things, but that's fine.

Decision: copy the entire project tree (except .git, bin, and large files) to /var/www/html. This matches the guide exactly (folders at the top of the docroot + HTML pages + the examples directory as a "proper use case"). bin/ contains CLI tools and node_modules — not needed by the web server. .git is not needed.

Then adjust the config:
- /var/www/html/config/baseConfig.json → set elasticsearchBaseUrl to http://localhost:9200 (already correct), proxyUrl to null (already correct).
- baseConfig_withProxy.json → set proxyUrl to the actual nginx URL: http://localhost/php/dataExplorerProxy.php. And update the PHP proxy to point at ES localhost:9200 (already hardcoded to localhost:9200 — perfect).
- Note: the guide says to adjust "the index name and base URL." The base URL http://localhost:9200 matches the ES I've installed.

CORS for direct access: ES 7 has CORS disabled by default. For pages that use baseConfig_noProxy.json (csvParse.html, plausibilityCheck.html, elasticsearchIndexAdministration.html, fcd pages, kosis pages) — the browser will need CORS. Two options:
1. Enable CORS on ES for localhost origins (ES 7.17: http.cors.* settings — enabled by default! Let me confirm: in ES 7.x, http.cors.enabled defaults to true! Actually, that's right — since Elasticsearch 7.0, CORS has been enabled by default with http.cors.allow-origin as… let me try to remember. Default in 7.x: http.cors.enabled: true, allow-origin: "http://localhost:*"? Hmm.

From the ES docs (7.17): "http.cors.enabled: Controls whether the CORS preflight check is enabled… Default: true." "http.cors.allow-origin: Configures which origins are allowed… Default: http://localhost:*." "http.cors.max-age: Default 1728000." "http.cors.allow-headers: X-Auth-Token". "http.cors.allow-credentials: false."

So by default, CORS is allowed from http://localhost:* — meaning direct access from a browser on the same host will work. The web server will also be at http://localhost (same host). So direct access should work without any changes.

But wait — there's still the mixed content / browser check issue… it's all http on localhost, so no problem.

So, to be explicit, I'll set the CORS config in elasticsearch.yml:
http.cors.enabled: true
http.cors.allow-origin: "http://localhost:*"
http.cors.allow-headers: "X-Requested-With,Content-Type,Content-Length,Authorization"
http.cors.allow-methods: "OPTIONS,HEAD,GET,PUT,POST,DELETE,TRACE"
http.cors.max-age: 1728000

Then create a test index with sample documents (e.g., "cities", with population and location) and run the following verifications:
1. curl the nginx page (200)
2. curl an ES search against that index via nginx proxy (PHP)
3. curl ES directly
4. Optionally, run a headless browser test to confirm that the JS initializes and populates the index selector. I could install a lightweight approach — e.g., a node + puppeteer download (a ~300MB Chromium download). That might be heavy, but it would give strong evidence. First, let me see how far I can get with curl-based verification. The core of the installation is: the web app is served by the web server and can reach ES.

Actually, a headless browser check has value as "objective evidence that the software is correctly installed" (the app's JS runs). Let me try puppeteer with the bundled Chromium — the container has plenty of disk space. First, let me try to verify with curl.
